author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Use blending, mipmapping, deinterlacing, and GS fixes correctly
summary: Understand what four commonly confused graphics controls actually change, then apply the smallest game-specific correction with a visual baseline and a clean rollback.
heroAlt: Native and upscaled rendering comparison from a PCSX2 graphics investigation

blocks.text: Four controls solve four different problems

Blending accuracy approximates how the PS2 Graphics Synthesizer combines framebuffer values; mipmapping selects texture levels as geometry recedes; deinterlacing reconstructs display fields; manual GS fixes alter specific hardware-renderer assumptions. They can influence the same final frame, but they are not interchangeable quality sliders. Changing several together can make one symptom disappear while introducing a harder one elsewhere.
Use the automatic or default mode for each control until a verified game-specific reason exists. Prefer a GameDB/known fix over a copied settings list with no serial, renderer or comparison scene.

Capture the fault at native resolution and with default GS settings. Identify whether it is transparency/order, texture shimmer, combing/interlace, or geometry/offset. Confirm the exact game serial and renderer because fixes for a regional revision can be wrong for another executable.

items: Verified dump and exact serial.
Default renderer settings at native resolution.
A screenshot or short recording of the repeatable fault.
No unrelated texture pack or post-processing filter.
Knowledge of how to reset the game's graphics profile.

blocks.text: Change the control that owns the symptom

items: 1. For missing or incorrect transparent effects, raise blending accuracy by one level and compare cost and correctness.
2. For distant texture shimmer or wrong texture-detail transitions, test mipmapping without changing blending.
3. For comb-like motion edges or vertical jitter, cycle the supported deinterlacing modes while viewing motion rather than a paused frame.
4. Use manual GS fixes only when an authoritative compatibility note names the exact fix and game serial; apply one fix at a time.
5. Retest native and the intended upscaled resolution, then save the minimal correction as a per-game profile.

blocks.text: The correction must fix the target effect without breaking unrelated scenes, menus or FMV playback. Compare multiple camera angles and at least one later area. Measure sustained speed because higher blending accuracy can be much more expensive than a simple resolution step on some GPUs.

items: Target symptom is gone in two cold runs.
No new missing effects or texture seams appear.
FMV and menus remain properly deinterlaced.
Performance remains full speed after warm-up.
Only the necessary control differs from defaults.

blocks.text: Reset the game's graphics profile when the cause becomes unclear. Reproduce at native resolution again, then reapply only the last proven correction. If software rendering is correct, preserve that fact in notes rather than copying every hardware fix into the profile.

items: Return blending, mipmapping and deinterlacing to automatic/default.
Disable all manual GS fixes.
Remove the texture pack or post filter used during an invalid comparison.
Restore the previous per-game profile backup.
Effect fixed but speed collapses: blending level is too costly for the device.
Shimmer persists at native: may be original game behaviour, not upscaling.
Static screenshot looks correct but motion combs: deinterlacing must be judged in motion.
Fix works for another region only: serial or executable revision differs.

blocks.text: Accuracy tuning works best as a diagnosis tree. Name the artifact, prove the responsible subsystem, apply one narrow adjustment and keep the evidence with the profile. That process yields a smaller, faster configuration than the familiar approach of enabling every GS fix in sight.
